Silber.et: From Middle High German silber, from Old High German silbar, from Proto-West Germanic *silubr. Cognate with Dutch zilver, English silver.

Silberfischchen.et: Mid-19th century, from Silber (“silver”) + Fischchen (literally “little fish”), which latter had already been used in this sense on its own. As in English silverfish, the name is based on the somewhat fish-like form as well as movement of the insect.

Silberfisch.et: From Silber (“silver”) + Fisch (“fish”). In the name of the insect a backformation from Silberfischchen, itself an extended form of older Fischchen.

s: a female given name, equivalent to English Silvia

He didn’t mention me even in one syllable.
Silbe.et: From Middle High German silbe < sillebe < sillabe, from Old High German sillaba, borrowed from Latin syllaba.

silbern.et: From Old High German silberīn, from Proto-Germanic *silubrīnaz.

s: a diminutive of the female given name Cäcilie [=Cecilia], from Low German or West Frisian

Silvester.et: From Pope Silvester I, whose feast-day has been the 31st of December since the Gregorian calendar reform of 1582. Compare Russian Сильвестров день (Silʹvestrov denʹ), Polish sylwester.

silbrig.et: From Silber (“silver”) + -ig. Cognate with Hunsrik silvrich.
